title: Psalm 74: The Sanctuary in Ruins
summary: The community cries out because enemies have smashed and burned God's sanctuary and there is no prophet to say how long the ruin will last. The psalm asks why God has rejected his flock and remembers his ancient victories as King, when he divided the sea and crushed Leviathan. It ends by pleading with God to remember his covenant, protect his afflicted people, and rise up to defend his cause.
story: Psalm 74 is the first community lament of Book III and follows directly after the personal crisis of Psalm 73. There the speaker found clarity by entering God's sanctuary; here the sanctuary itself lies in ruins. The psalm stands with Psalm 79 and the book of Lamentations as Israel's response to the destruction of Jerusalem and its temple, the greatest catastrophe in the Old Testament story. The promises of Psalm 72, a king whose reign would last as long as the sun, now meet the reality of the enemy's axes and fire.
historical:
The heading reads “A Maskil of Asaph.” Maskil is a term of uncertain meaning, possibly a psalm of instruction or skill, and Asaph was the founder of a Levitical guild of singers (see Psalm 73). Since the psalm describes the burning of the temple, it can't be from Asaph himself in David's day; it belongs to the guild's later repertoire. Most scholars connect it with the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC, when Nebuchadnezzar's commander Nebuzaradan burned the temple, the palace, and the houses of the city (2 Kings 25:8-9). Some have instead proposed the time of the Seleucid king Antiochus IV, who desecrated the temple in 167 BC, pointing to the complaint that there is no longer any prophet (verse 9), a lament also found in 1 Maccabees. Against that later date, the psalm describes the sanctuary burned to the ground, which fits the Babylonian destruction better than the Seleucid desecration, and the Psalter was probably largely complete by the second century BC.

Verse 8 says the enemies burned every place where God met his people in the land. Some older interpreters took this as a reference to synagogues, which would point to a late date, but most scholars now think it refers to local sanctuaries or to the temple courts and meeting places, since synagogues are not clearly attested in the land before the last centuries BC.
cultural:
Temples in the ancient Near East were believed to be the dwelling of a god, and the destruction of a temple was often interpreted as the defeat of that god by the conqueror's gods. The enemies' banners set up as signs (verse 4) were military standards, often bearing the emblems of foreign gods, planted inside the sanctuary as a claim of victory. The carvings smashed with hatchets and picks (verse 6) were the carved paneling of cedar and gold that decorated Solomon's temple (1 Kings 6:18, 29).

The images of verses 13 and 14 come from ancient Near Eastern mythology, where the sea and its monsters represented chaos. In texts from Ugarit, a city on the Syrian coast, the storm god Baal defeats Yam (Sea) and a many-headed serpent called Litan, a name related to Leviathan. The psalm borrows that imagery to say that the LORD, not Baal, is the true King who conquered chaos, both in creation and in the exodus, when he divided the sea. The dove in verse 19 is a picture of Israel as weak and defenseless, easy prey for wild beasts.
literary: The psalm is a communal lament built around questions: Why (verses 1 and 11) and How long (verse 10). Verses 1 to 11 describe the destruction in painful detail and plead with God to act. The center of the psalm, verses 12 to 17, turns abruptly to a hymn celebrating God as King from ancient times, repeating the emphatic word You seven times in the Hebrew as it lists his acts in creation and the exodus. Verses 18 to 23 return to petition, framed by the word remember (verses 2, 18, 22). The structure sets present devastation against past victories, and the hymn in the middle becomes the ground for the closing appeal: the God who conquered the sea can surely defeat these enemies.

outline.t: Why have You rejected us? Remember Your people
The enemy's destruction of the sanctuary
God the King who conquered the sea
Remember Your covenant and defend Your cause

doctrines.note: Verse 20 asks God to consider his covenant. The people's plea rests not on their merit but on God's commitment to them, which they call on him to honor even when the evidence seems to point the other way.
The hymn of verses 12 to 17 confesses God as King over sea, day and night, seasons, and the boundaries of the earth. The disaster doesn't cancel his rule; it drives the people to appeal to it.

The psalm gives the community words for collective grief and bewilderment, including the absence of any prophetic word. It shows that God's people may bring national catastrophe to him with honest questions.

words.note: Zakar, to remember. It frames the psalm (verses 2, 18, 22). When the Bible asks God to remember, it doesn't imply he has forgotten but asks him to act on what he knows, to keep faith with his people and deal with his enemies.

Netsach, forever or perpetuity. The psalm opens by asking why God has rejected his people forever, and it recurs in verses 3, 10, and 19. It expresses the fear that the ruin is permanent, a fear the psalm refuses to accept.

Livyatan, Leviathan. A sea creature that appears in Job 41, Psalm 104:26, and Isaiah 27:1. In this psalm it is a many-headed monster of chaos crushed by God. Israel used the image to confess that nothing in creation rivals God.

Berit, covenant. It is the binding relationship God established with his people, with promises and obligations. In verse 20 the people ask God to look to it, trusting his faithfulness more than their circumstances.

christ: Psalm 74 isn't quoted in the New Testament, and its link to Jesus is thematic. Jesus himself foretold the temple's second destruction, which came in AD 70 (Mark 13:2), and he spoke of his own body as the temple that would be destroyed and raised in three days (John 2:19-21). The psalm's cry for God to remember his covenant is answered in the new covenant Jesus established in his blood (Luke 22:20). And the confession that God is King who crushed the chaos monster finds its final echo in Revelation, where the ancient serpent is defeated and the sea is no more (Revelation 20:2; 21:1).

hard.q: Why does the psalm use pagan mythology about sea monsters and Leviathan?
hard.a: The psalm draws on images that Israel's neighbors used in stories of their gods defeating chaos. Some readers are troubled by this, but most interpreters see it as a deliberate claim rather than a borrowing of belief. By taking the language of Canaanite myth and applying it to the LORD, the psalm says that the powers other nations feared or worshiped are nothing before Israel's God, who alone is King. Some take Leviathan and the dragons as poetic figures for Egypt and Pharaoh, since the next verses speak of dividing the sea (compare Isaiah 51:9-10 and Ezekiel 29:3). Others see them as images of chaos at creation. Either way, the language is poetry used to confess God's sovereignty, not an endorsement of the myths it echoes.

questions: The people ask God to remember his covenant when everything seems lost. What promises of God do you hold on to in times of loss?
The psalm moves from lament to remembering God's past acts and back to lament. How does remembering what God has done help when he seems absent?
Verse 9 grieves the lack of any prophet or sign. How do you live faithfully when God seems silent?
